impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not included in its earlier IPR petition, and what evidentiary standard applies to determine whether a skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have been expected to discover the prior art.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's estoppel ruling, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous proof that prior art references were reasonably discoverable through diligent search.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers retain broader ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions, as courts must carefully assess whether prior art was truly discoverable and avoid hindsight reasoning in applying estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in using IPR estoppel to shield their patents from invalidity challenges in district court, potentially increasing litigation costs and exposure to additional prior art arguments.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody headache treatment patent claims were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury's findings that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were not invalid. The decision is significant for the pharmaceutical industry as it addresses the scope of written description and enablement requirements for genus claims covering antibody therapeutics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from a more permissive standard for patent validity of antibody claims, supporting broader patent protection for biologic drug platforms where the specification discloses known methods of making claimed antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face stronger patent barriers when challenging biologic patents that claim broad categories of therapeutic antibodies.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck VLSI's damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement on extraterritoriality grounds, affirmed in part on other grounds, and remanded for further proceedings. The decision addresses important questions about the territorial reach of U.S. patent claims for multicore processor technology and the adequacy of damages contentions disclosures.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against multinational technology companies benefit from the court's more expansive view of when U.S. patent infringement occurs despite some overseas components of the accused conduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations face increased exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims, and must carefully manage damages contentions to avoid exclusion of expert testimony.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in its assessment of damages models for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from broader acceptance of damages methodologies, including models measuring the defendant's enrichment, and from the reinstatement of jury-determined contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face significant trade secret misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages exposure under expanded damages theories on remand.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet filed its trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow for hiring former Insulet employees who allegedly shared proprietary information about insulin patch pump technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and district court judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The decision clarifies that the limitations clock begins running when the plaintiff knew or should have known of the misappropriation, even if the full scope of harm was not yet apparent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation through employee hiring benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's statute of limitations, providing a strong defense when plaintiffs delay filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation by departing employees; delays in filing suit risk forfeiture of DTSA claims regardless of the magnitude of the misappropriation.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that each of the asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed on trade secret claims, holding that plaintiffs failed to prove the asserted information qualified as protectable trade secrets under California law because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, ruling that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions for co-inventorship claims. The counterfeiting liability and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against trade secret claims benefit from the court's rigorous application of the requirement that trade secrets not be generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry; otherwise, both trade secret and related patent inventorship claims may fail.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Enanta's patent claiming compounds for inhibiting coronavirus replication could claim priority from an earlier provisional application where the provisional contained an alleged typographical error ('C2' instead of 'C1') in a substituent definition, and whether Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl group definition was not an obvious typographical error that could be corrected to preserve priority. Because Enanta could not claim priority from the provisional application, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated all claims of the patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from clarity that competitors cannot retroactively correct patent specifications to capture compounds disclosed between provisional and non-provisional filing dates, protecting freedom to operate for products disclosed in the interim.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face significant risk from even minor errors in provisional applications, as typographical mistakes in chemical definitions may destroy priority claims and leave patents vulnerable to anticipation by intervening disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the bond requirement pending appeal. The claim construction ruling reinforces branded pharmaceutical patent protection, while the bond ruling ensures generic competitors are protected from wrongful injunction losses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the court's claim construction affirming that the weight-to-weight ratio covers the salt forms used in commercial products, strengthening patent enforcement against ANDA filers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies face injunctive barriers to market entry, though the requirement of a bond pending appeal provides some financial protection against wrongful injunctions.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data patents are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door to attorney's fees for the defendant. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in the agricultural technology space face significant § 101 hurdles.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against agricultural data patents benefit from the confirmation that claims reciting conventional data collection and processing steps on known hardware are patent-ineligible, and may recover fees if the case is found exceptional on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech patent holders face heightened risk that patents claiming automated farming data systems will be invalidated under § 101, and may face exceptional case fee-shifting exposure.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the facts, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment regardless of the witness's personal knowledge and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's functionality in the sale. The court also held that computer source code is not hearsay because it constitutes machine instructions rather than human assertions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony and confirmation that commercial sales of devices trigger the on-sale bar without needing to publicly disclose the device's internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges where prior art devices were commercially sold but their internal workings were not publicly disclosed, expanding the scope of invalidating prior art.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that asks a single infringement question covering multiple patents requires a new trial, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis of building automation system wireless communication patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all asserted patents was prejudicially erroneous because it prevented identification of which patents were infringed. The court also remanded for further § 101 proceedings on the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for other patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately address infringement for each patent, preventing ambiguous verdicts that could inflate damages across unrelated patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face increased procedural complexity and the risk of new trials if verdict forms do not adequately separate findings for each asserted patent.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement, along with other exclusionary rights, has constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to independently sue for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license—possesses sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The decision clarifies standing requirements in patent cases involving complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving the right to sue, providing greater flexibility in licensing while maintaining enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot as easily avoid patent suits by arguing that the patent owner's exclusive license divested it of standing, reducing a procedural defense option.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied LG's motions on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for certain patents while affirming it for others, and affirmed the denial of LG's motions on infringement and damages. The decision provides guidance on the § 101 eligibility analysis for patents covering signal processing innovations in digital communications standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications standards space benefit from affirmance of eligibility for claims tied to specific technical implementations of non-uniform constellations, and from affirmance of infringement and damages findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the mixed eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about which communication technology claims survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether 'executable program code' limitations in patent claims directed to mobile device multimedia navigation should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), applying the framework established in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration under the intervening Dyfan precedent regarding when software claim terms invoke § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment. The court affirmed the jury verdict of invalidity for the '638 patent under § 102.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the court's instruction to reconsider whether 'executable program code' terms necessarily invoke means-plus-function treatment, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness under the updated Dyfan framework.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent claims face renewed uncertainty about claim scope when courts must reassess § 112(f) applicability under evolving precedent.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patent claims, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation can file IPR petitions on the statutory deadline of a party to that litigation, potentially circumventing the time-bar of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination for challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raises significant questions about third-party IPR petitions filed at the statutory deadline of a litigation party, implicating potential abuse of the IPR system.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the court's scrutiny of potentially coordinated IPR filings by non-parties and from vacatur of the Board's invalidity finding, protecting patent portfolios from procedural gamesmanship.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR as a cost-effective patent challenge mechanism face heightened scrutiny when filing petitions near statutory deadlines, particularly where coordination with litigation parties may be suspected.
